subtopic: STATUS OF CERTAIN EX-SERVICE MEN FORMERLY EMPLOYED AT NATIONAL STEEL CAR PLANT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STATUS OF CERTAIN EX-SERVICE MEN FORMERLY EMPLOYED AT NATIONAL STEEL CAR PLANT
speechtext:
I wish to make a very brief statement in connection with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that I had been somewhat discourteous in not supplying him with information. I should like to advise of the circumstances that gave rise to the hon. gentleman's complaint.
Last evening the hon. member for Cape Breton stated that no answer had been given with regard to the situation of certain inspectors trained in the National Steel Car Corporation at Hamilton.

Shell Inspectors

I had thought, Mr. Speaker, that the answer given in the course of debate completely covered the questions raised and had no indication from the hon. member that a further statement was required from me.
Reference to Hansard of March 19 last will show that after the hon. member had spoken the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) explained the reasons for setting up the intergovernmental inspection board and he said that while he was not familiar with the facts mentioned, and that the board conducts its own operations, he would bring the hon. member's representations to the attention of the board.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) was familiar with the situation and dealt with it on page 1698 of Hansard, pointing out that the inspection board required to use more numerous inspectors and for this reason had opened a training school at the National Steel Car Corporation plant. It was understood that these men would not necessarily be employed in that plant and they had given an undertaking, on completion of their training, that they would go to any plant in the United States or Canada, to which they might be directed.
The question of jurisdiction was also raised but I considered that an answer had been given in connection with the question of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) as reported on page 1699 of Hansard.
Any statement I can make would be almost entirely repetition. However, any additional facts might be briefly these:
1.	Twenty-one of those trained refused to leave Hamilton and rather than do so decided to be released.
2.	Positions were offered them in a plant situated near Montreal and the board agreed to pay transportation expenses and allowance, both for the inspector and for his family and effects.
3.	Later on an offer was made to transfer some of the inspectors to Lindsay but these refused to leave Hamilton, preferring to take chances of securing employment there.
4.	No female help is called on to replace male inspectors. Women employed by the inspection board are not employed as inspectors but as examiners, whose duties are of a routine character.
I do not think there is anything I can usefully add to this statement.

I should like to add a little to the question of shipbuilding, which took up the time of the committee for some time last evening. Four types of ships were mentioned during the debate, but I got rather mixed up on account of the way in which the debate jumped from one type of ship to another and some of the evidence that came out.
The first of the four types mentioned was the Fairmile. I will no-t discuss that type except to say that, as most people know, it is a fast motor boat, developed, I believe, mostly on the Muskoka lakes, on Georgian bay and perhaps along the east and west coasts. It is not a large boat. As the minister said, teak and mahogany enter into their construction. I am not going to discuss that type of boat, but I do wish to say something about the other three types mentioned-the corvettes, the mine-sweepers and the cargo ships. Corvettes are now built, I believe, on both coasts and principally on the great lakes. I know they are at Toronto. I have seen them at Fort William, Midland, Collingwood and Kingston.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: On the river.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
At Kingston, at the foot of lake Ontario. The question was raised as to whether they could be made in Nova Scotia. In my judgment, they can be. As to whether the steel can be purchased down there, I am not sure, and it is about the production of steel, having in view a long range shipbuilding policy, that I wish to say a few words to-day.
There is at New Glasgow a mill that rolled steel. I have not been able to find out the thickness of the steel rolled there. I have been told it is a quarter of an inch, but that might not be thick enough for either corvettes or mine-sweepers. There is no reason, however, why the capacity of the mill cannot be increased in order to roll heavier steel if the government so desires. I have been informed that they roll only up to 50-inch plates, and that would not be wide enough even if it were thick enough for corvette

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
hulls. The plate rolled there will do for various parts of the ships-stays, keel base, and so on. The hull plates themselves used in corvettes are made out of 54-inch plates reduced to 51-inches. I believe that largely 60-inch plates are used in the construction of mine-sweepers; and, as regards the cargo boats, anything in smaller size would be used for stays, and all the other inside steel work. But the plate itself on the outside of the ship is usually anywhere up to 84 inches. I endorse what my leader, the minister and others have said in this matter. If it is possible to establish a long-range plan of operation in Nova Scotia for the construction of cargo boats, I would be in accord with that plan one hundred per cent.
For the next few minutes I shall confine what I have to say to Nova Scotia. I know there is a large steel plant at Sydney in that province. I used to know its capacity in earlier days, but I have forgotten what it was. I believe that at the time of the first great war the mill was satisfactory for the production of steel plate. It is my understanding that plate is not now being made at the Sydney mill. I have never heard of any reason why it could not be manufactured there. Of course we realize that climatic conditions enter into the construction of steel plate. Whether steel plate is not being made at Sydney because of climatic conditions I do not know, but if the government could further a long-range plan to reequip the mills at Sydney and New Glasgow to build plate of the size required for corvettes and minesweepers, and particularly for cargo boats, I am sure the house would be in accord.
Why is this not being done? Although I am not familiar with the set-up I do know the company making steel at Sydney either controls or is able to get all the iron it requires from Bell island, not far from St. Johns, Newfoundland. I have been there, and I know the situation. The iron available at that point is good, and the deposits are among the largest in the world. I believe they have in sight about three and one-half billion tons of iron ore. That ore can be easily taken out and shipped.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: All under water.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, all under water, but easily taken out and easily shipped. The facilities are excellent for loading the iron into cargo boats. The distance from Bell island to Sydney is not far, and it is a water route.
Then around Sydney I presume there are ample supplies of limestone, a factor essential to the production of steel. There are ample supplies of coal-again among the largest in the world. Nova Scotia, therefore, with its 14873-132}
coal, its limestone easily obtainable and its iron ore easily transported, would be a natural place for the production of steel. So that if we are compelled, as we may be, to go into the building of cargo boats in a large way, it would seem that Nova Scotia would be a proper place in which to do it. Cargo ships can be built only on either coast and along the lower St. Lawrence in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Thousands of these ships will be required after the war, if indeed they are not required before that time. When we see our enemies scuttling their ships in the United States harbours we are led to the conclusion that they have at last determined that the only way they can beat the British empire is to prevent ships from arriving at the ports of the United Kingdom. It is for this reason no doubt that they are so anxious to destroy the ships of their own nationals in United States harbours.
It would' seem therefore that the government must meet this problem and must decide with respect to a long-range production of shipping. In the event of its deciding on such a programme Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would be excellent places in which to build those ships. We know that in the Glasgow area the ships are all constructed along the river Clyde. There must be many equally excellent berths in the maritime provinces for the building of ships, and plants could be erected near those berths for the fabrication of necessary parts.
Then the question of equipment arises. In the constituency of St. John-Albert there is one of the finest brass manufacturing plants in Canada. I refer to the McAvity plant, one I have known for twenty-five or thirty years, and one which within my knowledge makes first-class equipment. So that in the mari-times they have at least one great plant, and there may be more, capable of supplying large quantities of the valve and fitting materials necessary to complete the building of the ships.
Of course Ontario is the great manufacturing province of Canada-and likely always will be, in spite of what anybody else may say. It is a province of which I am very proud. I am proud, too, of the business men in Ontario, and I am certain they would be able and willing to supply large quantities of the necessary equipment. They do now, in fact. They will be in a position to supply steel too when it is necessary to have it fabricated in sizes thicker and wider than those turned out in Nova Scotia. We ship steel from Ontario to all parts of Canada.
Then, in Ontario we build marine engines. I am not sure whether engines of the desired
2092	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
size are made in Nova Scotia. Cargo ships are equipped with low-speed engines, capable of developing a propelling force of about ten to fourteen knots an hour, the speed of the ordinary convoy. Because of the comparatively low speeds required, the engines are not as large as they otherwise would be. No doubt they could be made in Nova Scotia. In any event they are now made in Montreal and Toronto. In my younger days the plant of the John Inglis company was not only a boiler plant but was known for its production of marine engines. I am told they are now manufacturing steamship engines again in that plant. If they are doing so I am certain the engines will be of good quality. It would seem therefore that there would be no difficulty in securing engines for the ships either in Toronto, or at points on the coast.
In my discussion of this long-range plan I now turn to the west coast. Within a hundred miles of Vancouver are iron deposits. I am told that limestone and coal are to be found in close proximity. I am told that they are not rolling plate on the west coast. If that is so, then I do not know why they are not, because it is being rolled farther down the Pacific coast, at Seattle, Los Angeles and San Francisco. The same could be done on the Canadian Pacific coast. I would suggest that in a long-range plan for the west coast there should be equipment to roll plate for themselves. What they cannot roll we in Ontario could supply.
I was happy to learn that yesterday the new steel plant at Hamilton of the Steel company of Canada, capable of rolling up to 100-inch plate, began operations. How much they rolled, or whether only a test was made, I do not know, but if it was only a test it would seem that they have reached the point of production. That is an important development in Canada. In addition to this plant there is the other great steel plant in Hamilton, Dominion Foundries & Steel Limited, which has been rolling plate for years. I am not thoroughly familiar with all their output, but I do know that they roll up to 78 inches. That would be plate of sufficient size for cargo ships.
We have in Canada, therefore, ample production capacity for everything entering into the building of a ship. Greatly increased demand may necessitate the production of steel plate in Nova Scotia and British Columbia, where the cargo ships will have to be built. The great lakes lend themselves particularly to the construction of the two smaller types, mine-sweepers and corvettes. There is ample capacity there to build anything required of these types. These ships are of a size that 
would go through the St. Lawrence canal. I believe that canal will take ships up to 250 feet, depending upon the construction of the bow and stem.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
This supplementary war
appropriation bill is to provide $135,000,000 in addition to the $700,000,000 which was charged against the consolidated revenue fund on March 31, 1941. Nearly all these appropriations are handled by order in council without any additional legislation. Fifty-two

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
boards have been appointed by the government of the day to control man-power, food, munitions and the actual conduct of the war. In addition to this cumbersome list of boards, we have parliament with all its powers and privileges, and added to that we have eighteen public departments, each with its minister and deputy minister. Every day new boards are being appointed by order in council to spend more money. We have the advisory economic board which is supposed to be the brain trust, and in addition we have boards to deal with coal, fish, dairy produce, bacon and so on. Last but not least, of blessed memory, we have the rags, bones and bottle board.
This is the occasion when members of the house are able to ventilate their war grievances before this money bill is passed. This is a money bill, and it is when such a bill is being discussed that we are permitted to air any grievance regarding the conduct of the war. I am sorry we have not the same rule as they have in the British house. I have before me the British Hansard for December 3 last. Instead of a prolonged debate on questions like this, they have a question and answer period on matters of great national importance, almost every day, from a quarter to three until a quarter to four o'clock. During that time members may ask questions about the war, and supplementary questions also, cross-examining the ministry. In this particular Hansard eight pages are taken up in a discussion on the orders of the day, about the non-delivery of parcels. Such a procedure eliminates prolonging the debate from day to day. It is charged thalf parcels do not reach prisoners of war in Germany, and that a private agency fails to distribute them.
There are two or three grievances which I wish to mention while this bill is under discussion. The first has to do with a matter relating to the department of the Minister of National Defence. I have great admiration and respect for the three defence ministers and anything I say will be in the form of constructive criticism. We seem to have learned nothing from the great war. Take the record office for instance. The militia department cannot tell us how many soldiers enlisted from Hamilton or from Toronto. Toronto seems to have been the stamping ground for recruiting officers from the Pacific coast to Halifax. That is all right and I am not objecting to it, but we should be able to get information. Last July the city of Toronto was requested by the head of No. 2 district to allow an appropriation for three or four clerks for four weeks to go over the records to find out how many soldiers came from Toronto.
The record office should be up to date like any other department of government. The Canadian Pacific railway and other large corporations work on the unit system, but here we are in the second war and we are using the same old system. The municipality should be able to get this information because it is necessary to prepare for the time when the troops come home. The same thing applies to all the civilian departments. It took me three or four days to find out something about the federal revenue collections from the city of Toronto. I was not able to get it from the minister's department, but last evening the Toronto Telegram contained a report from the customs head of Toronto that over $93,000,000 had been collected in customs, about ten per cent of this being from a subsidiary port which is now tacked on to that city for seme unknown reason. This is no way to conduct a public utility. It is high time there was a change in business methods. These departments should be conducted from the commercial aspect just the same as the railways and other large public corporations are conducted, and the amount of business done recorded on a unit basis.
Some of this money is to be used for the purpose of aiding the erection of munitions plants, but Toronto is not getting its fair share. The only plants we have are the Anaconda Brass, Massey-Harris, John Inglis, Dunlop Tire, Goodyear Tire, Hepburn, Dominion Bridge and a few others. Toronto is the logical site for munitions plants because it has a ready supply of raw materials, labour and power. The government is trying to conduct its business with old-fashioned methods. In the first years that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power, this country spent only $36,000,000 on maintenance and capital expenditures, but to-day we provide, by two bills, for almost a billion dollars to be spent by order in council. Yet we have the same old system which was used forty or fifty years ago.
We should have the unit system which is used by private corporations like the Bell Telephone and the railroad companies. That is how they conduct their business. The government has spent nearly $9,000,000 on public buildings in the city of Ottawa. I am not objecting to this expenditure, but this city is not of sufficient size to handle the volume of business in peace time, let alone in war time. In order that economy may be effected, some of these public departments should be removed to nearby cities. Then the ministers would be able to effect considerable economy which they cannot under the present system.
2094	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
There has been an agitation in the other house to take some of the work off the shoulders of members of the Commons, and that is the proper thing to do. The other chamber could deal, for instance, with some of the soldier problems and have a committee sitting from day to day. Ini Great Britain they are doing a great deal of war work in the House of Lords, and the same is true of the senate at Washington. In Great Britain they have reformed their whole parliamentary procedure to divide the work up between the two houses, but we have learned nothing in that line since the great war. I am of opinion that the business of parliament should be reorganized in such a way that the other chamber will be given more work to do. We need real parliamentary cabinet and law reform here in war time.
I wish to refer to one or two soldier matters because this is probably the last opportunity we shall have to bring them to the attention of the house. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has told us that since the passing of the lease-lend bill this government has not had time to do anything in the matter of bringing about parity between the Canadian and the United States dollar. Washington-minded as we are in Ottawa, the government have not even attempted to garner any of the fruits that should flow from the work which Canada has done for the north American continent as a pioneer in its defence. We all have a great respect for that great country to the south, but some of the people over there forget that for two hundred years the mother country protected their shores, enabling them to become the great industrial nation they are to-day-something everybody is happy about.
Last week we sent down to Washington a number of financiers. But what do these clerks, office boys and stenographers know about high finance, or peace and war, economic and international affairs in dealing with Henry Morgenthau, secretary of the United States treasury? The time has come for us to take up with Washington in a serious way this question of parity or near parity of the dollar, because to-day we are importing $40,000,000 worth more of United States goods than we did last year on which exchange has to be met. As I said last night, one can go into any of the large departmental stores of this country and see, on the counters, piles of United States goods, almost all of which could be manufactured in Canada, thus saving exchange. True, we have a treaty, a trade one, which expired last year but is kept on. I hope that something will be done about that, because, after all is said and done, the lease-lend bill applies to Canada as well as to our allies, China and other countries. This matter should
be taken up in a big way and certainly be referred to in the coming budget, and a wartime agreement made and entered into as an economic necessity for stability.
I have a letter here from the personal services officer of the Canadian Legion war services, stating that a soldier of the Ontario Regiment at Camp Borden is apparently about to lose some property which represents his life savings. The soldier is expecting to leave shortly for overseas and is much concerned as to the outcome of an action which is pending to dispossess him of this property. If he loses it, the writer says, his chances of rehabilitating himself on his return to civil life are very doubtful. The writer enclosed twenty-six papers, which I have transmitted to the Minister of Pensions. I should like to see a moratorium on mortgage foreclosures declared in respect of the property of all members of his majesty's forces, to continue in force until eighteen months after the war, during which period there should be no foreclosures of soldiers' property, and where necessary the government should pay interest, charging it against the soldier's mortgage at a low rate, when he returns. I hope something will be done about the matter.
There is another question to which I referred the other day in the hope of securing some measure of redress for this soldier grievance. I refer to the charges for meals on trains. Our military training camps are far-flung from Vancouver to Halifax, and I should like some of the members of this house to come ind see what Camp Borden is like with the water, rain, mud and all that kind of thing at this time of the year. The same conditions can be seen at Petawawa and other camps. We have spent between $9,000,000 and $10,000,000 on the camps, and I maintain that the soldiers should have been encamped near a city where sewerage, water supply, good roads, transportation and other conveniences which are a charge on the overburdened taxpayers would be available. What was the need of establishing camps at Newmarket, for instance, and Long Branch? Why do we need camps there when the Toronto exhibition buildings are available? Toronto has spent $24,000,000 on those buildings, grounds and permanent exhibits, and the soldiers could have been trained there and used the buildings in inclement weather. That would have permitted training to go on all during the winter without interruption. I do not blame the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) because I know he is a man of wisdom and great capacity, and he was not in charge of the department when all this was started, but I object to some of these expenditures as being secondary, not primary. The

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
battle of Britain is the vital thing. If that is lost and the battle of the Atlantic and the battle of the Mediterranean are lost, freedom and liberty are gone so far as the north American continent is concerned, and life will not be worth living unless we win the war.
With regard to the price of meals, we have in this building a cafeteria where one can get a big dinner for thirty-five cents, but a poor soldier travelling across Canada in inclement weather has to pay from $1 to SI .25 for a meal on the train. That is what they are charged by our two great railway corporations.
I wish hon. members could see some of the boys on the public ownership road. I have complained in this house before with regard to these conditions. I complained also because the rules of the house were broken when a committee was appointed, without notice first being given on the order paper, to consider the annual budget of the national railways and merchant marine. The soldiers are fighting the battles of this country, and they may never come back, and they should have free fares from the railways, for all the federal aid they have had.
I have a return here showing what the Canadian Pacific Railway has received month by month for transporting soldiers, and in my opinion it is this corporation or the two railways which are the real authors of the hitch-hiking orders which have been issued. I know something of that matter from the returns which have been brought down and from what I have read.
This return also shows what was paid to the Canadian National Railways, which my former leader called a dead-head railway, and that is what it is. Everybody seems to have a pass over the road if he has pull. Lindbergh got a life pass, not just a pass from Camp Borden home. The return shows that the Canadian Pacific Railway received for the transportation of navy, army and air personnel in September, 1939, $78,000, in round figures; in April, 1940, $323,000; in September, 1940, $289,000; in October, 1940, $373,000. Altogether, from September 1, 1939, to February 28,	1941, that railway company received

The Canadian National Railways received for the same period a total of $2,573,226.28.
The Canadian Pacific Railway, no matter what government is in power, always has the biggest pull of any corporation in this country. One only needs to be a member of parliament and attend the committees of this house to learn something about that railway. There is no doubt that they have done a great deal for Canada, and their services in war time could not be surpassed by any great corporation in the world, but I do ask that
railway to give some consideration to six poor soldiers who stole five or six tickets costing about $18.90, especially when it is remembered that the railway got from the government $2,628,000 for transporting troops to camps all over this country, since the war started.
Turning to another matter, I challenge the right of any commanding officer of a camp, without the authority of parliament, to issue orders on the camp notice board making certain actions within the law taken by soldiers a military offence. Let me read these four paragraphs:
Railway tickets and bus tickets must be purchased and handed into company office before 1200 hours Fridays. These tickets must be attached to the passes and given out at 1600 hours.
Personnel proceeding by privately-owned motor cars must inform the C.S.M. of the name of the owner of the car, also the car licence number, before 1200 hours on Fridays.
Do not get the idea that you must go on pass every two weeks.
If you have not enough money-do not go. Save your money.
I have a letter protesting against these instructions. They are illegal and without authority. The Fairbanks branch of the Canadian legion writes me:
Hitch-hiking is not the proper way a man in the king's uniform should travel, and we think the government ought to be big enough to provide a decent means of doing so.
Every effort must be made to allow these men to visit their homes and loved ones while they are in Canada, because some will be a long time gone after they leave these shores.
Too much cannot be done for the boys who are willing to go over there for their country, and we have faith in the government that it will do something.
Some of the commanding officers are more reasonable than others with regard to applications from those who wish to be officers. In my opinion all officers should come from the ranks. I understand that the former commanding officer of one of the corps of engineers has given a ruling that nobody who has not had university training or graduated along those lines can get a commission.
Another matter which might be referred to is the inaction of the government with respect to enlisting the cooperation of members of parliament. So far as the Toronto district is concerned, I doubt whether any hon. member has ever been invited to attend a single camp or anywhere else to see what is being done or is hoped to be done by the government from 1940 to 1942. The only letter along these lines which we have had, so far as I know-and I have asked some other hon. members-came from the Department of National War Services, asking us to take part
2096	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
in a "scrap" campaign. I have pointed out on another occasion that this work is covered, so far as our city goes, by the police commission and licensed peddlers. It is also handled by the Salvation Army, who have big trucks going to every house in Toronto to collect the week's scrap; by the Poppy day fund, which have a regular service also, and raised by this means a large sum of money to take care of its work; by some of the women's organizations, including the Imperial Order, Daughters of the Empire; by the National Council of Women; and last, but not least, by the street department. Then, why any further duplication of services? That was the only invitation we have received. It was dated March 17, which was probably a good day to send it out, because some people born under the colour which that date symbolizes are, in any event, very full of "scrap." Anyway, that is the only invitation we ever got, to go out and collect rags, bones, and bottles, and I suppose we got it because some of us are "Conservatives," although the government is supposedly conducting a "Liberal" war.
In my opinion the small loans act operates against the interests of our soldiers. At the pawnshops where they try to raise a few dollars, they are charged rates away in excess of two per cent a month; in some cases, up to three or four times that amount. These men should have protection, if needs be by some measure brought in by the Department of Finance to assure them a little better consideration or a lower rate under federal authority.
Another matter to which I wish to refer is the situation in respect of the buildings at the camps. It seems that at least three or four departments have charge of these buildings. The Minister of National Defence, who is always illuminating and informative, brought down a splendid report upon the cost of these camps, but some of the work is done by contract, some by the department of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, some by the Department of National Defence and the air force do a lot themselves. No doubt it was a rush job and the work W'as necessary.
I am making no objection to it. But as regards the Department of National Defence for Air, I have in mind that at the foot of Yonge street to Sherboume street on the Queen's quay, in Toronto, a large number of wooden huts have been constructed, and I have received many complaints from carpenters and builders and others in the district that they cannot get employment on this work, but that people from all over Canada have been brought in to do it, nobody being taken on who is over forty-five years of age; further, that the rates and labour conditions are not 
what they should be. I reported the matter to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and his director of public relations-I do not know what that phrase means, because every department seems to have a "department of public relations"-

speechtext: Poor relations!

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
-simply referred me to the commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force at Toronto, and his public relations branch. What is the idea of having these huts? As we go past, we see a large number of troops doing nothing except guard duty enough to protect a city hall, and all they do is to protect lumber which is already protected by the city police, by the harbour commissioners, and by the contractors. No wonder there are so many people in the unit suffering from throat trouble, as the return to an order of the house showed.
I have in mind another matter which should be looked into in the interests of recruiting and of the army in general. I want to find out about the large number of civilians who are doing nothing in the army but sitting in offices, wearing uniforms, and getting-some of them- double pay-men in the city of Ottawa for whom the Ottawa river is the first and last line of defence so far as the war goes. I have received a number of communications objecting to the use of civilians in the Department of National Defence, while returned soldiers are out of work. They complain regarding the "number of uniformed men in the naval department who are merely doing the work of clerks, but who first secure commissions as lieutenants, thus enabling them to draw military pay on civilian jobs and to wear naval uniforms." Some of these lads were never on a coal barge, to say nothing of any other craft; they are not like the able "admiral" we used to have here from the bay of Fundy, who was a real authority on the sea and shipbuilding. "They will perform civilian clerical duties only until the war ends, but instead of drawing $75 per month as clerks, they will draw lieutenant's pay and allowances."
Another objectionable feature is the press bureau of the Department of National Defence for Naval Sendees. The other day I got a magnificent booklet, or brochure, or album; there is nothing like it on the north American continent, although it emanates from what is known as the "silent arm of the service."
Did you ever hear, Mr. Chairman, of the Royal Navy making up a book of photographs of itself and sending them all over the country as a publicity stunt? I am here to pay tribute to the noble courage of the men who are writing a glorious record on land, sea and

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
air; the history of courage is being rewritten by them, and I. particularly congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Air on the good work he is doing. But one feature of the work of these departments simply does not appeal to me at all, and that is the large number of people who have been engaged for publicity work. As I pointed out five years ago, when this matter of naval protection was under discussion and I was urging a national shipbuilding policy and the opening up of all shipyards to prepare for a vast merchant marine policy before it was too late, and that something be done, we found that at the last shipping conference and the previous imperial conference the Dominion of Canada sided with two other dominions, and did not side with New Zealand and Australia in an advanced, forward empire shipping policy to rebuild the merchant marine. We would not assist or give one dollar towards the Singapore base, and we said, at the last empire shipping conference, that as far as the Dominion of Canada was concerned, we had no commits ments and did not intend to make any towards maritime freedom. I do not see why the departments should be loaded up with all these publicity people. It is ridiculous to have these civilians-for that is all they are-walking up and down Yonge street in Toronto, or Sparks street here, wearing the king's uniform.
I do not blame the three ministers in charge of this department for these conditions; they have made many improvements; but why should these people, who really are only civilians and wear uniforms, enjoy increased rates of pay, while the men who are going overseas, privates and N.C.O.s, have to salute these gentlemen who are simply sitting at home getting double rates of pay for working on publicity, pay branches, and similar civil service jobs in the various departments at Ottawa and not in actual war work? Why, the streets at times are filled with many of these people 1 One has only to walk into any hotel rotunda or departmental store in Toronto to see many of them. The ministers in charge of these departments, who know far more than I do about these matters, are capable men and no doubt are trying to make some changes. I suggest that there should be some division in this matter of personnel; that those officers who are performing only civilian duties on the staffs of various departments should not wear the uniform at all, unless enlisting for any theatre of war, and the returned men should fill these positions.
Regarding publicity in general, there is no doubt that Canada is not being properly advertised in the United States. I hope that
parliament will take note that on the next St. George's day, the day we celebrate in honour of England, there is to be a visit by Mr. Menzies, the splendid Prime Minister of Australia. Australia is opening an office in New York which will operate as an information bureau and will supply data on all phases of Australian life and on what that commonwealth has done in the war, and Australia has a great story to tell of her war work. That bureau will deal with the press and put on a real publicity campaign, giving them proper information instead of some of the garbled information that is coming into Canada now of war and foreign affairs.
I have here a letter from a leading head of a big store in the west end of Toronto, complaining about our information bureau. He says he has written several times asking the head of this department not to send him any more of this information because he cannot distribute it; it just goes, he says, into the waste-paper basket. In view of the great shortage of paper in Great Britain and this country, he thinks this waste is regrettable. I think the point he makes is well taken.
This bill will be the last opportunity we shall have to go into all these questions. I wish to commend the government for a great deal of what it has done, especially during the last year, but I would direct its attention to one or two matters which should be looked into. One is with regard to British prisoners of war. I have here the British official Hansard of Tuesday, December 3, 1940, in which there are three pages of questions and answers, beginning at page 392. It is charged that owing to the United States having been more or less against Germany, the former policy under which the United States government looked after the distribution of Canadian Red Cross parcels and private parcels to prisoners of war is no longer being attended to. The British government was asked as to its intentions with regard to these privately run enterprises. They did operate through Lisbon, but now, since the lease-lend bill, it is difficult for them to do anything, or get Red Cross parcels delivered.
These parcels are not arriving. The following members took part in the debate: Captain McEwen, Mr. Law, Sir William Davison, Viscountess Astor, Major-General Sir Alfred Knox, Miss Ward, Mr. Lees-Smith, Mr. Robert Gibson, Mr. Bellenger, Sir Adam Maitland; and the reply is given. The government here should also look into this situation. If the British government are not delivering the parcels, how can we know with regard to any private organization in Canada who send parcels? We had the head of the Y.M.C.A. in America telling us here last fall

2098	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
that parcels were being delivered by the Y.M.C.A. He came here from the United States to give his views. The debate in Britain is to the contrary. This, I believe, is an authentic report of the proceedings in th'e British house, and this question is creating a great deal of anxiety among the relatives of our own troops. I have had several letters from mothers and fathers and wives of these men wanting to know if they get the parcels. Sir William Davison said:
... I hold in my hand a letter from a prisoner in Oflag VII camp, dated October 29, saying no Red Cross parcels of any kind had come to that camp . . .
The minister said that there was a great deal of difficulty due to shipping and the changes that had taken place, and deliveries were difficult. An inquiry should be held into the matter at once, and I refer the government to these pages of the British Hansard for a complete statement of the case. Action should be taken.
Another matter with regard to these prisoners of war is that when they are in the army they are allowed so much a day and sustenance. When they become prisoners of war they do not get any allowance, and they do not get proper clothing, although by our law they are still on active service and should be paid. The country should pay for it. There is discussion of that in the same Hansard. I hope the government will look into it. They pay for food and clothing and they do not get it, Hansard says.
Another matter is that the information the country is getting, both on the radio and in the press, is not what it should be. The proceedings of this house are not reported. I heard the other day a man on the BBC giving his views, and it is time we had a Who's Who so that we may know who these people are, even the BBC, that are giving Canadians information about the war and about this bill and other matters. One of the broadcasters is J. B. Priestley, one of the best-known pacifists Britain ever had, who, for some unknown reason, got this job. Here is what he said in 1938:
The most dangerous lunatics we have had to do -with in this century have been the "be prepared" agitators. ... All those people who go about saying that war is inevitable, and giving us their views on the next war, are either dangerous lunatics or criminals. They ought to be locked up and fed on bread and water.
One has to understand who these people are and then one can know how much attention at times can be paid to them because they \yere wrong all the years before the war. So when we are told that parcels are being delivered, the authority for those state-

ments should be looked into, and a survey made as a result of America not being now able to function in Germany.
This supplementary bill and the main war appropriation, reaching a total almost unthinkable, are the net result of the sham sort of world Canada lived in from 1921 to 1939. They thought of nothing but Geneva and all its works, and threw away not only our defence but our friends. They also misjudged the whole European and domestic situation. We were told that there would never be any more war and that a bill like this would never be necessary again. We were told that on all sides of this house; that is the result of pacifism, disarmament, Geneva, Stressa, Locarno, Kellogg pacts and Munich. Had we made ourselves secure and been prepared, we would not have had a bill for one-third of this amount. But this bill to-day, what is it? It is just preparing the way for the Marxian theory; it is simply heading for the totalitarian state. The ministers take pride in the magnitude of the figures, the dizzy height; it has almost gone up to the height of the tower of Babel, in geometrical progression, and they are very proud of it. But there has been altogether too much taxation, too much of the methods of the big stick, too much telling the people of Canada what they are going to do next fall and winter and all kinds of scarecrow publicity. The late Hon. J. Israel Tarte said "elections are not won by prayers"; and to wait until you see where Canada will be next year in taxes. With the present ministry and all the professors, we shall in time reach a totalitarian state. There never was a time in the history of this country when a vigorous opposition was more needed than it is to-day. Wait until you see how your bread and tea and groceries will be taxed next year; see how we are going to take from Mr. Hepburn and the other provinces and the municipalities the gasoline tax and the motor vehicle tax, with all the scarecrow and big stick methods. There never was a time when the opposition had a greater opportunity. The London Economist said recently:
The fact is that an alternative administration in opposition-able and willing to become a government, but with no wish, real or professed, to disrupt the state itself-is a necessity of sound democratic government. Indeed, one of the chief items in any really satisfactory reconstruction of the post-war world would be the emergence of such an opposition, and certainly not its suppression. In the event, of course, the advocates of a straight] acketed "unity" and the place-seekers may conceivably have their way, for it is hard to see where a real opposition is to come from; but it would be a setback, not progress.

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
In short, what is wanted in our public life is not the blurring of outlines but their clearer definition. It is no gain to have a formula which misrepresents two opposite views. It would be much better to have both defined.
They refer to what is proposed for reconstruction afterwards. The government would be well advised to adopt the principles laid down in this British Hansard; if they did, the debates would not last half a day or a day, and allow an hour daily for questions and subsidiary questions on all features of the war and crossexamination of the ministry, thus giving the country the facts and preparing it for the difficult days ahead.

speechtext:
Last night I intended, when the discussion centred on Nova Scotia, to say a few words, but I did not have an opportunity then. Since the subject has been brought up again this afternoon by the hon. member for Davenport, I wish to make a few remarks.
The hon. leader of the opposition said last night he wanted the government to put Halifax back on the map. Halifax is on the map now, very much on the map. A couple of weeks ago I was in that city for a few days and what I saw there proved to me that Halifax was definitely on the map. If every member of the house had a chance to go there, he would see what has been done by the government and it would convince him much more than by looking up figures, listening to complaints and voicing them again in this house. While in Halifax, I spoke to people in every walk of life. I admit that the conversation at times came back to the shipbuilding programme and the contracts that had been granted in Canada; but at no time did I hear, while I was in that city, such bitter complaints as we heard here at times last night. On the contrary, instead of complaining, most of the people I met in Halifax were proud of the role played by their city in the present war, and of the use made of the facilities of their wonderful harbour.
With regard to the explanation given by the minister last night as to this question of shipbuilding, I confess I am not an expert. I was not born on the Clyde, as was the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). I was born on the shores of the St. Lawrence where there was no shipbuilding industry, in a beautiful, small city, Riviere du Loup, whose people are ably represented in this house by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). That city, by the way, has supplied to this present parliament six members, who are past or present citizens of that city

the 14873-133}
Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), the hon. member for Temiscouata, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lizotte) and the member for Bellechasse.
Although, as I was saying, I was not born on the Clyde, strangely enough I was able last night to understand the clear explanation given by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) in such masterly fashion. Even in Halifax, most of the people I met, although some of them expressed the wish that more could be done if possible in that part of the country, understood the reasons which were indicated to the committee last night by the minister. One afternoon, after visiting the historic buildings that house the local assembly, I was invited by a hospitable Haligonian to his club. The reasons given by the minister last night were also voiced there by some business men. They said, "We have to admit that this is the position. We should like to have the specifications so drawn up that we could fulfil them, but we understand that they were put there not by Angus Macdonald but by the British government." So they admitted that the person responsible was not the minister; they understood that it was not the Canadian government but the British government that gave the specifications and that those specifications had to be complied with. It may have been hard for them to swallow, that they all tendered too high, but they understood the reasons that have been given by the minister.
As regards steel shipbuilding yards, the minister said there was only one. I was even privileged to visit this yard and to see the work that was being done there, and it is much more important than any new plan of shipbuilding. I am not at liberty to explain, but it may be inferred from what I say, that the work that is being done in this Halifax yard at the present time for the Canadian and the British governments is of much more importance than the building by this yard of one or two ships a year.
While there I had an opportunity to visit the British naval base. I am not at liberty to describe what I saw, but it was a heartening sight. I wish that more members could go there. They would better realize the situation. A visit to Rear Admiral Stuart Bonham-Carter would inspire anyone. He is a genial man and a fine personality. Coming in contact with a person like this makes one understand the success of the British navy. These men can be calm before and after battle, as shown by Admiral Cunningham who, after winning the last victory over the Italians, took his family to the moving pictures at
,100	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
Alexandria. They are the sort of men who control the British navy, men who can be charming and entertaining on occasion, while being authorities in their own sphere.
I also had an opportunity to visit the Canadian naval base under Commodore Jones, and here, again, I was most favourably impressed. The Canadian navy has been enlarged tenfold. It is extraordinary to see what has been done in such a short time. It is a remarkable achievement, and it has been accomplished within a few months-because, after all, we cannot count in terms of years. Only a few months have elapsed since the start of the war, and such a change has been brought about in the Canadian navy that one must actually see it to realize what has been done. One must see it on the spot. Here, we simply look at figures and we hear of so many new ships and so many men; there you actually see what has been accomplished and you realize, more vividly than the reading of figures and statistics can make you realize, the change that has been brought about. This is due to the far-sightedness of the Department of National Defence, of the ministers, past and present, and mainly to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, who has given so much attention to the programme of the construction and expansion of the navy.
While I was there I visited the headquarters of the eastern air command under Air Commodore N. R. Anderson. Again, I am not at liberty to say much, but I can say that what I saw there is indeed remarkable, the coverage made by the air force, vast areas, their activities in so many ways, the wonderful organization they have within headquarters. You have to see it to realize what is being done. When you are there you realize that the petty criticism that is indulged in amounts to nothing. Some people will say that this has not been done and the other has not been done, but when you see it in actual operation you realize what the government has done. If more hon. members would go there they might be ashamed of voicing some of the petty criticism that we hear from time to time. They would see the magnitude of the work done.
I also visited Dartmouth air port under Group Captain A. L. Morfee. It is a splendid achievement both as regards material and as far as the men are concerned. They have a much larger number of men than I imagined, men not in transit overseas but defending the eastern portion of Canada. They are working for the defence of our own countiy. I suppose I can say that the achievements of the air arm so splendidly organized by the air ministry, are due, to a large extent,

to the ' dynamic personality of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), who must have inspired his men, because a tremendous amount of work has been done and the men and the organization are thoroughly efficient.
I am not supposed to speak for Halifax; I have no brief to do so. I can tell the committee, however, something of what I have seen, and I think it would be well if others could see for themselves what the different branches of the Department of National Defence have done. It is heartening to see the material effort of Canada centralized in the activities that one sees in the harbour of Halifax. The few shortcomings can be excused in view of the shortness of the time in which the government has had to expand these facilities.
Someone referred the other night to the housing condition. I understand that this is being remedied. A number of houses are to be built under the housing programme and barracks are being erected so as to avoid the troubles complained about. I understand that barracks cannot be erected fast enough. If the expansion of such a programme is under consideration, I would advise that many more barracks be constructed for men in the different services.
Then, there is talk there about health services. Perhaps I might be permitted to say to the Minister of Pensions and National Health that the wish of the majority of the population is that one central authority should act in that connection. His department should get in contact with the provincial, municipal, army and navy health authorities, and get their consent so that there would be one central authority with power to apply regulations to prevent unhealthy conditions in Halifax.
In conclusion, may I state that Halifax is indeed a great city, a city full of enthusiasm for its war effort. Haligonians are proud of the men who hold three of the most important portfolios in the cabinet. In this regard I may say that while I was lecturing at Dalhousie university the chairman of the evening, referring to Dalhousie and Laval universities, stated that if the graduates of Dalhousie and Laval were withdrawn from the government, the administration would be crippled. It would mean that the Minister of Justice, the three Ministers of National Defence, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State would be withdrawn.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) suggested this afternoon the advisability of formulating some policy whereby, after the war is over, shipbuilding in Canada might be continued. May I add my voice to that of the hon. member in that regard? When this war began we did not have sufficient capacity in our shipyards to supply the demand. We learned, and we have known for many years, that ships can be built in Great Britain for about fifty per cent less than they can in Canada. If therefore the shipbuilding industry is to be continued in Canada, as I believe it should, it will be necessary for some government to formulate a plan of assistance to shipbuilding. In time of war, when there is a heavy demand -in fact when the demand is greater than the supply-we are warranted in giving shipyards contracts at prices higher than those which could be justified in time of peace. Therefore if we are to see to it that the shipbuilding industry does not at the conclusion of the war decline almost to the zero mark, where it was prior to 1935, it will be necessary for some government to formulate a plan.
I am keenly interested in this matter because in my constituency of Simcoe North we have in Collingwood one of the largest shipbuilding industries in Canada. Before I came here as a member of this house in 1935 I came to Ottawa with a deputation from that district to interview the government. On that occasion we urged upon the government the necessity of formulating some plan to keep a certain nucleus of men working, so that if the time did come when it was necessary to do some shipbuilding the men would be available for that purpose.
A few days ago the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) asked why the Collingwood shipyards were not working more than one shift a day. No doubt the hon. member felt that if there was a demand for ships, a larger demand than we could supply, the shipyards should be working more than eight hours a day. Discussing the matter with officials of the Collingwood shipyards I learn that they have sufficient orders. They
have orders ahead, and all they can handle at present. But if they changed from one shift to two or three shifts they would do so only at the expense of other shipyards in Canada. They require expert men in the building of their ships. They feel therefore that it is better gradually to build up their supply of skilled men, and to have those men trained in their own industry, rather than go out and draw them from other industries already engaged in the war effort.
I would urge upon the government, at this time when shipbuilding is urgently needed, the necessity of formulating some plan under which when the war is over we shall not be caught where we were three or four years ago, with our shipyards almost empty and with a lack of skilled men to work in them.

I should like first to make a few observations respecting what was said by the Minister of Labour when the orders of the day were called at the opening of this sitting. He stated that I had described as discourteous his failure to answer my question at an earlier date. I had no intention of conveying any such impression. I have found the Minister of Labour always ready and willing to cooperate. I had pointed out only that the system followed by the Minister of National Defence in answering questions asked in the house was a system which all departments should follow as closely as possible. Several days had elapsed since I had brought the matter to the attention of the minister, and I considered it of sufficient importance to bring it to the attention of the house. I thought I should have an answer. The reply given this afternoon does not answer the question I had intended to ask, which was this: What efforts are being made by the Department of Labour to find employment for the forty-six men who are unemployed as a result of their being replaced by girls in the plant in Hamilton?
When these men entered the plant to be trained as inspectors there was an understanding or agreement with the Canadian government that in the event of their having to go to the United States or other parts of Canada to do that kind of work they would be paid a subsistence allowance. When they were called in and informed that they were to take similar work in other parts of Canada -and some of them in the United States- they wrere told that the subsistence allowance did not apply. They were to be sent out of the country to work at 56 cents an hour which was six cents an hour more than they were receiving in Canada. They were objecting, not because they did not wish to leave the country but because the subsistence allowance had been taken from them. As a result

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
they are unemployed. I wanted the Minister of Labour to tell me what he or his department had done with respect to securing employment for men over whom they should have supervision and jurisdiction.
May I speak briefly respecting the statement made by the hon. member who recently visited Halifax. He would convey the impression to the house that conditions in that city apply to the entire province of Nova Scotia. The city of Halifax is a very small part of Nova Scotia. Undoubtedly the city of Halifax is making a valuable contribution to the war effort, but compared with the rest of the province they are faring well. The majority of people living in the eastern part of Nova Scotia look upon Halifax as the end of Canada. It is the end of the radio chain; it is the terminal of the Trans-Canada Air Lines, and the harbour commission is there. Halifax is well taken care of and is very well represented so far as government is concerned; it is the seat of government. The conditions have been correctly described by the hon. member, but they certainly do not reflect the conditions that exist throughout the rest of Nova Scotia. I am glad he was so well received. He was taken to the historic chamber which houses the legislative assembly. He was certainly treated better than I was the last time I was there. I went there toward the end of December 1940 at the request of the executive board of the united mine workers, to take part in a coal conference called by the provincial minister of labour. When I arrived in Halifax I met the minister, but I was refused permission to take part in that conference. Apparently the hon. member from Quebec had more pull or exerted more persuasive powers upon the local authorities in Halifax.
I listened with interest last evening to the discussion of shipbuilding as applied to Nova Scotia. Two statements were made which stand out and which should form the basis for any discussion of this question. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services stated that at present the shipbuilding plants in Canada were not operating to full capacity and that there was no shortage of shipbuilding facilities. He said that until such time as the shipbuilding facilities of Canada were taxed to the full he did not see the necessity of the government subsidizing or forcing shipbuilding plants in Canada to take on orders. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) read a statement last evening which had been made by Mr. D. B. Carswell, the controller of ship construction and repairs in the Department of Munitions and Supply. I imagine that Mr. Carswell, whose duty it is 
to examine into these questions of shipbuilding, should know something about the proposition. He stated:
Principal problem facing an "all out" cargo and warship construction programme in Canada, which would involve establishment of new shipyards throughout the dominion, is the problem of finding the money for both ships and yards.
This statement on March 11 of the man charged with the responsibility of advising the Department of Munitions and Supply would indicate that shipbuilding is one of the major problems and perhaps one of the greatest contributions to our war effort that could be made at the present time. Yet on the other hand the minister, who of course was not speaking for his own department, makes the statement that shipbuilding plants in this country are not operating to capacity. Each of these men has a certain responsibility with respect to this particular question, but they have made opposite statements which should be clarified.
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) emphasized the fact that food is being rationed in Great Britain when we have an abundance in Canada. Of course the reason for the rationing is that we cannot get the food to England. The people in Britain are fighting our battle and one of our major problems is getting the necessary supplies of foodstuffs and so forth to them. These two statements would lead one to believe that either the controller of shipping or the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services is mistaken. It is not my intention to make an analysis of these statements; I merely call them to the attention of those in charge. Statements of this kind going out to the people through the medium of the public press lead the man on the street to believe that those charged with the responsibility of carrying on such an important part of our war effort are not using their best judgment.
I was disappointed also at the statement made by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services when he attempted to analyse the reason why shipbuilding has not been carried on more extensively in Nova Scotia. He pointed out that at one time shipbuilding was the major industry of this province. He said also that shipbuilding yards in Nova Scotia had been asked to tender, but that very few had even put in tenders, and those who did were twenty-five per cent higher in their prices than shipbuilding yards in other parts of Canada. He could give no reasonable explanation for this. The minister's statement amounted virtually to an accusation against the shipbuilders of Nova Scotia of sabotage or an attempt to obtain greater profits

Supplementary IFar Appropriation Bill
than other shipbuilders. In the light of the present situation I think that is a serious statement to make.
Personally I do not believe that any such thing is true. It should be clear to anyone who makes an examination of the set-up in Canada why the shipbuilders of Nova Scotia are not in position to accept orders. The shipyards in Nova Scotia are small and their owners are not able to expand them because they have not the necessary capital. The minister doubted very much whether the spirit of those engaged in this industry was equal to the spirit which had actuated the shipbuilders of seventy-five years ago. I think the same spirit is there, but the economic setup is different to-day from what it was seventy-five years ago. The industry lacks capital and it is not able to expand in order to handle the building of these ships.
Fifty or seventy-five years ago, when the shipbuilding industry in the province was flourishing, Nova Scotia controlled its own capital. At that time there were six or seven banks in the province-the Merchants bank, the bank of Nova Scotia, the Halifax Banking company, the bank of Yarmouth, the Commercial bank of Windsor and the Union bank of Halifax. These banks were all organized in the province and were ready to lend money for the carrying on of business. Through mergers the assets of these banks were transferred to Toronto. Eighty per cent of the capital invested in the manufacturing industry is concentrated in one province. The people of Nova Scotia no longer have control of their own capital.
You must have capital to expand. If you want capital the first thing you must do is apply for a loan. If the loan is for an amount over a certain figure the application must go to the head office in Toronto. You must state the reason why you require the loan. Generally the people who direct the banks are at the head of our manufacturing industries. If a loan is required to expand an industry in the eastern part of the country which will come into competition with one established already in Ontario, the logical thing to do is to refuse to lend the capital to expand that industry. I think this matter will be serious until such time as the government are prepared to take hold of this question of shipbuilding.
The plants in the eastern part of Nova Scotia wall have to be subsidized if it is absolutely necessary-and this is admitted by all-for us to produce the ships. And we should not stick to wooden ships. Press reports have stated that an attempt was made to start a plant in the eastern end of Nova Scotia. I think that should be followed up. As I stated the last time I spoke on this
question, if the government erected a plant and operated it themselves at no profit it would serve a twofold purpose; it would not only increase production but would provide employment for the many who have not employment to-day in the eastern end of that province. I think I am absolutely right in summing up the situation in this way, and I think the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services will admit-maybe off the record-that that is the true picture. The shipbuilders of Nova Scotia have been represented as people who are looking for enormous profits, but the actual situation is that control of our own resources in Nova Scotia has drifted into another province, into the hands of people who are not interested in creating in another part of the country competition for themselves.
The minister of naval services stated that so far it was not the intention of the government to subsidize the shipbuilding industry. But as the war is now developing, particularly on the sea, before very long ships will be the most important thing we shall need in the prosecution of the war, and the government would be well advised to take into consideration the question of subsidizing, where necessary, shipbuilding plants. According to the minister himself there are fifty in Nova Scotia.

speechtext: I must apologize for not having been in my seat last evening, but I had an important meeting with departmental, officers. I explained that it is well known to the department that there is a steel rolling mill at Sydney, which was established at the end of the last war, too late to be of use in that war. We have considered since the beginning of the war the desirability of putting that mill into operation, but the difficulty has been this, that the whole capacity of their ingot steel has been contracted for, and there is none available to turn into plate. What is the difference between a British contract and a Canadian contract?
I am simply asking the minister if that is the British contract to which there has been reference. There is no need for him to fly off the handle about the question.
Well, we always have great distinctions drawn as to whether we are building for Britain or for Canada.
I am merely asking if it is a British or a Canadian contract.

What I was trying to envision-if the minister did me the honour to read the few remarks I made last night-was the establishment of a national shipbuilding policy for Canada to be effective from now on and after the war. I think it is very important. The present programme is for Britain.

As a matter of fact a programme has been authorized for Canada. Unfortunately it takes time to organize an enterprise of this magnitude. A merchant ship costs around a million and a half dollars, and it is not sufficient just to step out of the door one morning and say, "I want to order ten of these ships." It takes a little prevision. But we have been studying the situation very intensely. The British government have spoken for the output of certain yards; and the Canadian government is going to have the output of the balance of the yards, and it is our intention to organize that output to the maximum extent which is reasonably possible.
Now we are getting somewhere.

I thought that in an earlier address I had made substantially that statement, because this project has been under way for some time.
We must organize not only the shipyards themselves but the raw materials, the plates, the boilers and engines, and all the innumerable fittings which go to make up a merchant ship. This is being done. We are studying sources of the required equipment. There is no use in building a hull if we cannot build a boiler which can be delivered to meet the hull when the boat is launched. The matter of brass fittings and other components of a merchant ship represents industries which must be expanded with the shipbuilding industry itself in order to prosecute a large programme of the kind. It is the intention to use existing yards to the fullest capacity, to build additional berths where
additional berths can be built and manned, and after that, and only after that, to explore the situation as regards new shipyards.
And the extension of the present shipyards.

Well, as I say, extension of present shipyards comes first. That is what I referred to when I spoke about building new berths for existing shipyards.
We have not ceased from the commencement of the war to expand this industry. Anyone who will cast a look at emplo3'ment figures in the shipbuilding industry will find that each month since the latter part of 1939 has seen a substantial increase in the number of employees in shipyards. We have expanded about as fast as we can expand, and therefore I suggest, because we have decided on an all-out shipbuilding programme, we cannot in a month double the number of men at work in the industry; it must expand as rapidly as possible, but in an orderly way. We must expand the supervision as we increase other types of labour, and that is what we are doing. We have had committees of experts on both the west and east coasts. The east coast committee arrrived back in town only last evening, and we shall have their report, as well as one from the west.
There is no difficulty about getting orders for boats. We have all the orders we can fill. There is no difficulty about steel. A modern plate mill of large capacity was started before the war and is coming into operation this month.

Will the minister permit a question? I learned-I hope it is not true- that in order to keep our present plate mills in operation we shall have to import ingots from the United States. Is that true or not?

If we have to, I think it is only a temporary situation. As my hon. friend knows, the ingot capacity at two of our large steel plants is being expanded very rapidly. I cannot say that there will not be a transition period when ingots must be imported, but we shall have a balanced operation very shortly, if not immediately.
We believe that we can expand boilermaking and engine-making facilities to meet requirements. That is being studied in a systematic way. We believe also that we can extend the facilities, which are at present overcrowded, for the making of brass ancillary equipment, so as to meet all requirements of that kind. But to approach a project of this sort, which will involve the expenditure of a great many millions of dollars, in any spirit but one of caution, would bring results,

We are placing this merchant shipbuilding in separate and, I think, most capable hands. I hope to be able to report in a day or two to hon. members the whole organization for carrying out the merchant shipbuilding programme, and I believe that the house will appreciate the fact that we have organized the operation on a very sound basis.
The matter of geography is, of course, important.
We have undertaken other programmes- for instance, a very large gun programme. Eventually guns will constitute about one-third of all the munitions made in this country.
Someone has said that we should have a shipbuilding industry at New Glasgow. I cite that city as an example, because it is being mentioned here. We are being asked to erect a great number of new houses in New Glasgow because the people engaged in industry there cannot find places to live. That indicates, it seems to me, a rather undesirable situation. It means that there has been a considerable transference of population from other locations to New Glasgow. To increase the congestion by adding yet another industry in that locality would, I assume, seem to all hon. members to be unsound.
We are undertaking in Halifax a large housing programme. That of course cannot be avoided, because there has been a large transference of population to the city from all parts of Nova Scotia. A great deal of activity centres in that area, and it must be the centre of an active ship-repairing industry. Almost every ship which comes into the harbour needs repairs of some kind, and we must have facilities there to effect those repairs promptly. Therefore it will I think be impossible to centre a great merchant shipbuilding industry at Halifax. To do so would mean further transfers of population to that point and a further considerable expansion in housing. I believe the people of Halifax themselves would consider such a mushroom expansion of that very fine old city a mistake. I am sure it would be in the long run.
Why not go to Saint John, then?

Well, in Saint John we are said to have a housing programme; we are not satisfied that that is the case, but there again we have a great deal of activity. Second to Halifax it is the busiest harbour in Canada ; in fact the tonnage passing through the harbour of Saint John is greater than that loaded at Halifax, for the reason that Saint

John is loading a great deal of bulk materials such as wheat and timber. We have at Saint John a shipbuilding industry and we are doting our best to expand it. We think it is possible to expand to a point where we shall be able to build merchant ships ini Saint John; we hope so, although there has been very little surplus labour for assignment to the small programme of corvettes that we put on in that yard early in the war.
I can say to all hon. members that we are exceedingly anxious to make this programme of merchant shipbuilding the largest that Canada can possibly execute. If on examination we can find any way of enlarging the programme on sound lines and with reasonable prospect of success, I can assure the committee that that avenue will be followed to its end.

I feel
greatly heartened by the statement just made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I wish to convey to him my thanks for the clear, succinct way in which he has laid before the committee in general terms what it is proposed to do. We shall watch with interest the development of this programme of commercial shipbuilding, and for the announcement which he said he hoped to be able to make in a few days.
May I remind the committee that this statement was in marked contrast to the statement made by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services last evening. On the one hand you have a sane, cautious statement of progress; on the other you have every evidence of defeatism.

The minister for naval services told us last night that they could build more ships here than they had the personnel to handle. I recall a statement being made in a broadcast from England that they had sufficient personnel over there to man the entire United States fleet if it were turned over to them.
