It just does not look so good, in fact it looks worse than it did before. The minister then went on to say:
-but I do not think it is of any use to make general observations like "every shipyard should be busy and all Nova Scotia shipyards should be working," when in some respects the yards themselves have not taken full advantage of the opportunities that offered.
To have a minister make that statement in the middle of a war is certainly pretty discouraging to the people of Canada. Every shipyard that can possibly be used should be used at this time. There certainly should not be any further delay.
The minister ended his remarks by referring to the hon. member for Weyburn in the following words:
If my hon. friend thinks we should take people by the throat and gestapo them into building ships when they do not want to build them, that is another story.
From the facts which have been presented, and having in mind the great urgency of procuring ships, having in mind the fact that we conscripted the youth of this country to fight-
When?

Do not ask me when or I may tell you. Right after the election is when. This government solemnly promised that they would not conscript people, but of course they did. Did not we have three cabinet ministers stand up in their places and say that they would resign from any government which put in conscription? Yet right after the election it was put in.
No.

The mere fact that a Liberal government break their word is not the question here; they have done
2112	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
it so often. The fact is that we have conscripted men in this war and under the authority of this government. These companies refused to do this work, or at least they did not do it, but they were coaxed and coaxed to do it. We coax industry to do work, but we pass the mobilization act to put our young fellows in the trenches. That is not playing fair with the people of Canada. There is certainly no equality of sacrifice in it.
You don't know what you are talking about.

If the hon. member will get up and talk it will be quite interesting to hear what he has to say about it. We should have an explanation from the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. He and the Minister of Munitions and Supply should get a little closer together on this thing.

May I interject just one or two remarks in connection with the statements made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat? There were reasons why the Nova Scotia yards did not bid on the Fairmile boats, and one reason was that they were not as well equipped to build that type of boat as the Ontario yards. I understand that the contracts for the Fairmile boats were let on the basis of an average price, taking a horizontal cut of the tenders given. These Fairmile boats, which are very fast, are made largely of mahogany. Spruce is the wood generally used in Nova Scotia for planking. There was no oak in Nova Scotia suitable for ribs or frames, so their timber would not be at all suitable for the construction of these boats.
Inspectors were sent down to investigate all that.

Learn something
about it.
I am tiying to learn from the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services.

I am simply trying to place on the record why the Fairmile boats were not built in Nova Scotia yards or anywhere else in the maritimes. The yacht yards of Ontario were especially equipped to build these boats and they had the organization and technicians available. They could build them to better advantage than could the yards in the maritimes. This is the main reason why the Nova Scotia yards did not tender on these boats.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to tell the committee the position of the department and the government in connection with this

particular matter which we are asking parliament to vote. I shall then have to leave it to the committee to decide what will be done about it.
The $135,000,000 which we are asking for by this bill should be-I was going to say "must be", but I do not think I have the right to say that-made available to the crown before the Easter recess at the latest. The same thing applies to the further supplementary estimates for the year ended March 31, 1941, which have been referred to the committee of supply. The consequence of either one of these measures going over beyond the Easter recess will be that accounts, many of which have been held up now for several weeks, will not be paid until the end of April or perhaps in May. If by any chance they went over until the Easter recess into the month of May, we would have to make special provision because there is only one month of grace for payment of the accounts of the fiscal year that is ended. I was hoping that the committee, having discussed pretty much the same matters on the main bill for several weeks and on this bill for quite a number of days, would now facilitate the passage of this measure.
There are some subsequent sections on which hon. members will probably want to say something, but I should like to make it clear that it would be a great inconvenience, not so much for the government as for the people with whom the government deals, if by any chance either of these measures should go over beyond the Easter recess without being enacted.
I hope that to-morrow and the next day further supplementary estimates may be placed before the house and that they may go through rapidly. I will give an undertaking that if any hon. member wishes to raise lateT on upon other estimates any question which should properly be raised under these supplementary estimates, I shall take no exception to their being discussed.
Mr. MaeNICOL:	But what about the
chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think the chairman would object if we had it understood among ourselves that it could be done. I say that because I should like to have these measures passed if possible before to-morrow night. I do not know whether we can pass this one before six o'clock this evening but I hope hon. members will cooperate in seeing that this measure passes before Friday night.

The minister was good enough to speak to me about this matter and I have given him my assurance that so far as the official opposition is concerned the government's proposals and

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
requirements will not be held up. The minister has given an undertaking that consent will be without prejudice to future discussion. But I do not see how we can pass this measure before six o'clock, because there is an important section of this bill, section 4(1) (e), and the interpretation that has been given to it, on which I desire to make some observations.
So far as we are concerned, the appropriation will be available before the Easter adjournment, by consent if necessary, on the undertaking and understanding that the minister has given. I give him that assurance now, but it will take me about half an hour to make the protest I desire to make in connection with section 4(1) (e).

There is one feature in
connection with this shipbuilding question which I think should be explained to the house either by the Minister of Munitions and Supply or by the minister for naval services. But before I point out this feature to the ministers I should like to say to the committee that fortunately I represent a seacoast constituency where they do build ships, and that I have been through several shipbuilding yards, so that perhaps there will not be the objection to my making a few remarks that there was in the case of some other members.
Last night I understood the minister for naval services to say that as yet there had been no money' advanced by way of capital advance to any shipyard. As hon. members know, over $300,000,000 has been advanced to different industries by way of capital advance for building plants, extensions to plants, and so on, but I understood the minister to say that nothing like that had been done in the case of shipbuilding yards. We have had complaints from members from different parts of Canada that advances of capital were required by some of the shipyards. I do not know whether that is so in British Columbia, but the suggestion has come from members in some of the other provinces. I do think therefore that the ministry should make it quite clear whether it has adopted the policy of not advancing money for the expansion of shipyards or for setting up new shipyards. Is the ministry prepared or is it not to advance money for these two purposes?
The Minister of Munitions and Supply stated this afternoon that our new shipbuilding policy is to build all the ships that can be built physically in Canada. I hope that that is correct, but his own controller of ship construction and repairs, Mr. D. B. Carswell, said in Vancouver just about three weeks ago, as quoted in the Vancouver Sun of March 11, under the heading "Lack of funds delaying ships":
Principal problem facing an "all-out" cargo and warship construction programme in Canada, which would involve establishment of new shipyards throughout the dominion^ is the problem of finding the money for both ships and yards.
This statement was made to the Sun to-day by D. B. Carswell, controller of ship construction and repairs in the Department of Munitions and Supply.
Then Mr. Carswell was asked the question:
Is there not some way this can be overcome? Germany seems to be building ships and other war materials without money. Why can we not do the same thing in Canada?
And Mr. Carswell's answer is significant. He replied:
That is a question the government will have to answer.
It is a question which I think the government should answer clearly. I have never been quite satisfied with the attitude of the Minister of Munitions and Supply with regard to merchant shipbuilding in Canada. Last year on June 14 I suggested to him-members will find the discussion at page 785 of Hansard that:
The present would seem to be a good time for Canada to inaugurate a steel shipbuilding programme.
That was last June. The minister's reply, the essence of his reply, was this:
Whether at a time like this we should divert the productive capacity of Canada to the peacetime operation of building merchant ships is, I think, questionable.
That was an amazing reply. I remember the minister more or less laughing at my making the suggestion that Canada should build merchant ships. I hope that he has had a complete change of mind since, and that he means it when he says now that Canada is going to adopt an all-out programme of shipbuilding. I believe there is no other question on which there is so much unanimity among the Canadian people as on an all-out programme of shipbuilding at any cost. They want every ship built in Canada that can be built, regardless of cost. Our distinguished visitor to Canada the other day. Mr. Wendell Willkie, made a clear-cut and definite appeal to the Canadian people which should be answered by the Canadian government when he said-I am quoting from the Ottawa Citizen of March 25:
I want to say to you, if I learned one thing in Britain it is that one of the keys to our victory depends upon the people of Canada, the people of the United States, supplying more and more ships.
Then he went on to point out what ships mean to Great Britain, and he said:
I plead with you, citizens of Canada, I plead with my fellow countrymen across the border, give every ship, give more than every ship, give
2114	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
more than every ship that is free and unnecessary, give ships until it hurts, keep them going, keep them going and victory, then, is sure.
To that appeal surely every Canadian says, amen. I hope the government will go all-out on this question. Perhaps the fate of our whole civilization depends upon whether or not ships can be produced in this western hemisphere, and I hope the Minister of Munitions and Supply or the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services will give us the definite, clear-cut assurance that Canada intends to go to the limit in building merchant ships, and that the matter of funds will not be allowed to hamper their construction.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I should prefer that the question raised by my hon. friend in the last moment or two of his address be answered by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply. He has made a statement here this afternoon, and if he wishes it amplified to-morrow to satisfy my hon. friend, he should, I think, undertake that duty himself.
With regard to the other question which the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) asked, namely, whether the government has assisted shipyards, my statement last night was that, so far as I knew, the government had not. I have not had time to verify that at the Department of Munitions and Supply, but I am convinced the statement is correct.
As regards the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), I endeavoured to make the position clear, and I am sorry if it is not clear to any hon, members. Roughly speaking, there are two kinds of shipyards in this or any other country. There are those which build wooden ships, and those which build steel or iron ships. Very seldom does one find that the same yard undertakes the construction of both types; they are two separate businesses. All the Nova Scotia yards are wooden yards, and the only warships which they can build are these small types of warships, such as the Fairmile patrol boats and wooden mine-sweepers.
That would not apply to Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I excepted Halifax for the reasons which I gave last night. The Halifax yards are quite capable of building steel ships, but they are busy doing repairs. The Nova Scotia wooden shipbuilding yards form part of a group numbering throughout Canada, I estimate, from fifty to seventy-five. On the great lakes and the St. Lawrence there must be more than forty yards capable of turning out yachts, Fairmile patrol boats and mine-sweepers. On the west 
coast are located many wooden shipbuilding yards. I therefore assume that there are throughout Canada from fifty to seventy-five wooden shipbuilding yards. But what the hon. member for Bow River has not grasped is that these wooden shipbuilding yards are of no value in the present cargo ship emergency. We must build cargo ships of a sufficient size to justify their being put into transatlantic use. What these small yards can do is to build yachts oir fishing schooners in peace time, and small boats in war time for naval purposes; that is, wooden boats about the size of the Fairmile craft.
The fact that certain builders in Nova Scotia did not undertake this work had no effect on the pace of the war effort in this country or in this empire. All that happened after the Nova Scotia builders, except one who took a contract for these Fairmile boats, were unable to undertake the work, was that we went to the builders on the great lakes and the west coast and said, "You do it." That did not in any way impede the progress or the speed of our war effort. It is as if my hon. friend went into a store in this city to-day and asked for a pair of boots of a certain style which the store did not have; presumably all he would have to do w'ould be to go to another boot store and get what he required. It is entirely wrong to endeavour to create the impression, as set forth by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, that the Nova Scotia builders are saboteurs.

He did
not say that.	.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, he said that. He said they could be considered either as saboteurs or profiteers, because either they were reluctant to help the war effort or they wanted to make too much money.

That is
not as I heard it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There are no more loyal people in this country than the people of Nova Scotia, including the shipbuilders; but anyone who has had to do with tenders knows that among even the most reliable contracting firms there will be variations in bids up to fifty per cent. One man may be better equipped, or may be a little more venturesome, or may have a better store of supplies on hand than another There are a dozen reasons which prompt one man to submit a lower bid than another. That does not indicate in any way that the latter is a saboteur or is indifferent to the war effort.

Defence of Canada Regulations
So far as the urgency of this matter is concerned, let 'me say that wooden shipbuilding yards in Nova Scotia or in any other part of Canada have nothing to do with the merchant shipbuilding programme. They can only undertake to build small boats, and the diversion of certain orders for these small boats from Nova Scotia to other yards has had no effect upon the naval programme of this country.
Progress reported.

subtopic: TABLING OP REGULATIONS RESPECTING PAYMENTS ON ACREAGE REDUCTION IN WESTERN PROVINCES

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: TABLING OP REGULATIONS RESPECTING PAYMENTS ON ACREAGE REDUCTION IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Before the house adjourns, I desire to lay on the table the regulations passed under the authority of the War Measures Act respecting payments in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and the Peace river district of British Columbia, of specified sums per acre on the number of acres taken out of wheat production and seeded to grass or coarse grains or summer-fallowed in 1941.
These regulations are of necessity not complete in that there are certain cases which will require to be dealt with on a basis similar to that which is finally decided upon in setting up quotas. A case in point is the occasional farm which grew no crop prior to this year. Such a farm is not covered in these regulations, but must be covered. There may be experiences necessitating further amendments in due course.
It has been stated by a number of hon. members that they would like to see these regulations referred to a committee for review and report. Some have suggested a special committee and some, the committee on agriculture and colonization. I am having the regulations distributed to hon. members this evening. It will be understoood that the preliminary work will of necessity have to proceed. If, however, hon. members after reading over the regulations think a committee necessary, I have no objection, but I would hope that the committee could sit immediately and complete its sittings if possible before the easter adjournment. The government has adopted the policy outlined in the regulations and feels it must be made effective at the earliest possible date.

subtopic: TABLING OP REGULATIONS RESPECTING PAYMENTS ON ACREAGE REDUCTION IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: A pretty vain hope.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TABLING OP REGULATIONS RESPECTING PAYMENTS ON ACREAGE REDUCTION IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
I should like to make this observation. I think it would probably be
desirable to have them referred to a committee, but, in the light of what we are doing in this house, with the budget to come down possibly on Tuesday, I do not see how it will be possible to have proper consideration given to these regulations between now and then.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, April 3, 1941.
